title: Bodhisattva Vows of Compassion
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the four Bodhisattva vows, beginning with the verse that jumped out from a book on a California bookstore's remainders table when Nomon was fifteen or sixteen. Drawing on Shohaku Okumura's Living by Vow, Nomon treats the impossibility of vowing to save all beings as the energy of the practice, then turns to Dogen's poems about bringing others across first and to the joyful, parental, and magnanimous minds from Dogen's essay on monastery cooking. The second vow brings in the kleshas and four pairs of opposites, such as praise and blame, and gain and loss. Nomon closes by reading Dainin Katagiri's poem "Peaceful Life" twice, then reminds listeners that "free all beings" includes themselves.

It was on the remainders table, which is the kind of book I'd be looking at.
I didn't have much money.
It was a book on Buddhism, and I just opened it at random, and there, offset amongst the regular paragraphs, was this verse.
It jumped out at me.

I vow to save them.

I vow to become it.*

Whether you knew it or not, by sitting here and walking and standing and chanting and bowing, you're enacting the living experience of a Bodhisattva.
So just to let you know what you are.

The mythos of it is that the Bodhisattva is a very serious and developed student of Buddhist practice, of meditation and so on, and could just keep merrily practicing away until they became completely peaceful and happy.

I don't know if the original word in Buddhism is exactly the same as renunciation.

I think we're all here actually practicing renunciation, which means letting go of something that my self-oriented me might want, in service of a greater good.
